summary.text: The report concerns collection-time parameter-ID generation failing with KeyError('__name__') when a parametrized value is an instance of a dict-like custom class whose __getattr__ maps missing attributes to dictionary lookups. An older issue, #6321, reports effectively the same symptom and class behavior, making it a possible duplicate.

known_facts.text: The reporter said replacing the custom wrapper instance with a normal dict allowed the tests to pass and that the same test had worked approximately one week earlier.
The reporter later identified the relevant implementation detail: the class assigned or delegated __getattr__ and __setattr__ to item access, causing a missing __name__ lookup to raise KeyError.

A maintainer explained that missing attributes should not produce KeyError through __getattr__ and suggested supplying an explicit parametrization ID, with the concrete example pytest.param(MyBroken(), id="broken").
The reporter said a workaround that restored normal behavior for attributes not already defined allowed the same instance to be used.
A maintainer requested a minimal reproducer, but none appears in the complete retrieved discussion.
The issue was closed on June 9, 2026; the available evidence does not establish that pytest code was changed or that any fix was released.

missing_information: A minimal, self-contained reproducer showing the custom class and the exact @pytest.mark.parametrize call.
The pytest and Python versions from both the last working environment and the failing environment, including what package or environment changes occurred during that week.
Whether adding an explicit ID to the parameter, as suggested in the discussion, avoids the collection failure in the reporter's environment.
content.draft_reply:
Thanks for clarifying that the parametrized value was an instance whose `__getattr__` delegated to dictionary item access. That means pytest’s attempt to inspect `__name__` while generating a parameter ID can receive `KeyError` instead of the `AttributeError` expected for a missing Python attribute.

The suggested `id` is part of pytest’s public parametrization API, not a modification to pytest internals. For example:

```python
@pytest.mark.parametrize("value", [pytest.param(MyClass(), id="custom-value")])
def test_value(value):
    ...
```

Alternatively, `__getattr__` should translate a missing dictionary key into `AttributeError`; the reporter indicated that restoring normal handling for undefined attributes also worked around the failure.

This also closely resembles #6321, which reported `KeyError: '__name__'` during ID generation for a parametrized dict subclass with custom `__getattr__`. If this report is revisited, please provide a minimal reproducer and the pytest versions from the working and failing environments so we can determine whether there was a separate regression beyond that existing behavior.
limitations: No source code, commits, linked pull requests, or releases were inspected, and no reproduction was executed.
Only the title and body of candidate issue #6321 were available; its comments and any historical resolution were not reviewed.
The duplicate search used the recorded query “getattr KeyError”; it found a strong candidate but cannot rule out other related issues.

comparisons.reason: Both reports describe pytest failing during automatic parameter-ID generation when a parametrized instance has a dict-backed __getattr__ that raises KeyError for the missing __name__ attribute. The evidence strongly suggests the same failure mode, although the target lacks a complete reproducer and version history needed to confirm it.
similarities: Both failures occur while parametrizing custom class instances.
Both trace the failure to pytest inspecting __name__ while resolving an automatic parameter ID.
Both involve dict-like classes whose __getattr__ returns item access and therefore raises KeyError('__name__').
Both reporters state that the behavior had worked previously.
differences: Issue #6321 supplies a complete reproducer and identifies pytest 5.3.1 as failing after pytest 4.3.1; the target does not provide comparable pytest version details.
The target mentions Python 3.14 through its installation path, whereas #6321 reports Python 3.7.3.
